results.proposed_proof:
**Given:** The finite FK laws for real $q\geq1$, their deterministic cylinder limits, and the finite torus RSW and influence interfaces in the cited suppliers.

[F1] Finite FK is positively associated, has the spatial Markov property, is increasing in parameter and boundary wiring, and has conditional edge-open probability at least $\rho=p/[p+q(1-p)]$ ([[lem-csm-frontier-fk-fkg-spatial-markov]]).

[F2] Numerical free/wired cylinder limits exist, are translation and quarter-turn invariant, obey parameter and boundary comparison, and agree outside an at most countable parameter set $J_q$ ([[lem-csm-frontier-fk-cylinder-pressure-comparison]]). These are numerical identities, not an assumed Borel extension.

[F3] Every fixed-aspect rectangle strictly inside a periodic torus has a uniform positive self-dual crossing probability ([[thm-csm-frontier-fk-torus-rsw]]).

[F4] The finite conditional-influence bound is that of [[lem-csm-frontier-fk-influence-threshold]].

[F5] Complement-edge planar duality has parameter $p^*/(1-p^*)=q(1-p)/p$ and includes the exterior-face convention ([[lem-csm-frontier-fk-planar-duality]]).

[F6] Opposite-direction grid crossings intersect, and simple polygonal circuits separate their bounded and unbounded components ([[lem-csm-frontier-grid-crossings-intersect]], [[thm-polygonal-jordan-curve]]).



1.1 For an increasing event $B$ on a finite graph, differentiation of its finite FK weights gives $\phi'_p(B)=\operatorname{Cov}_p(\mathbf1_B,|\omega|)/[p(1-p)]$. Writing $u_e=\phi_p(e\text{ open})$ and $I_B(e)=\phi_p(B\mid e\text{ open})-\phi_p(B\mid e\text{ closed})$ yields $\phi'_p(B)=\sum_e u_e(1-u_e)I_B(e)/[p(1-p)]$. By [F1] the coefficients have a positive lower bound on a compact parameter interval inside $(0,1)$. On an $L$-torus a translation-invariant $B$ has equal influences on each of the two edge orbits, each of size $L^2$. Thus [F4] implies $\phi'_p(B)\geq c\phi_p(B)(1-\phi_p(B))\log L$. Integrating its logistic derivative between $p_s$ and fixed $p>p_s$ shows that $\phi_{p_s}(B)\geq b>0$ implies $1-\phi_p(B)\leq C L^{-\eta}$, with constants independent of $L$. [F1, F4, algebra]

1.2 We specify the finite stopping operation used for an outer circuit. In a finite ambient box list all simple circuits in the annulus between $\Lambda_{r_{k+1}}$ and $\Lambda_{r_{k+2}}$ which surround the inner square. For a candidate $\gamma$, let $I(\gamma)$ be the edges whose relative interiors lie in its bounded component, including edges entering that component from circuit vertices. Let $O(\gamma)$ contain all other ambient edges, including circuit edges. The event selecting $\Gamma=\gamma$ is: every edge of $\gamma$ is open and there is no surrounding open circuit in $O(\gamma)$ whose bounded interior strictly contains that of $\gamma$. These tests involve only $O(\gamma)$. To verify that exactly one candidate is selected whenever a surrounding circuit exists, splice any exterior excursion of another surrounding circuit with the outer arcs of $\gamma$, keeping the unbounded face on the outside, and erase subloops not surrounding the inner square. This gives a surrounding circuit in the union, on or outside $\gamma$, with strictly larger interior if that excursion protrudes. Applying this finite operation to all candidates yields an outermost circuit; two different maximal circuits would enlarge each other by the same surgery. Equal interiors have the same Jordan boundary. Thus the selected candidate is unique. For each output $(\gamma,\tau)$, where $\tau$ is the full assignment on $O(\gamma)$, the output fiber is precisely the fixed-exterior cylinder $\{\omega|_{O(\gamma)}=\tau\}$ if $\tau$ passes the tests, and is empty otherwise. Every interior assignment is admitted. This fiber identity, rather than a claim about a particular probing order, certifies that conditioning on the output never conditions an interior edge. [F6, construct]

1.3 For $m\geq r$, reaching $\partial\Lambda_m$ entails $D_r$, and wired domain comparison gives $a_m\leq\phi^1_{m,p,q}(D_r)\leq a_r$. In particular $a_n$ decreases, so $\Theta^1=\inf_n a_n$ exists. Taking $m\to\infty$ in the displayed inequalities gives $\Theta^1\leq\pi^1_{p,q}(D_r)\leq a_r$. Infimizing over $r$ proves $\Theta^1=\inf_r\pi^1_{p,q}(D_r)$. This is a pair of real inequalities, not an exchange of two limits. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.4 On a finite edge set and for an increasing event $D$, its Hamming distance $H_D$ is the minimum number of closed edges to open to enter $D$. Opening one coordinate lowers it by zero or one; hence $|\omega|+H_D$ is increasing, $H_D$ is decreasing, and $H_D\mathbf1_D=0$. Finite differentiation and FKG give $\frac{d}{dp}\phi_p(D)=\{\operatorname{Cov}_p(\mathbf1_D,|\omega|+H_D)+\phi_p(D)\mathbb E_pH_D\}/[p(1-p)]\geq4\phi_p(D)\mathbb E_pH_D$. Integrate from $p$ to $t>p$ and use monotonicity of the decreasing $H_D$ to obtain $\phi_p(D)\leq\exp\{-4(t-p)\mathbb E_tH_D\}$. Apply this to $D_n$ in wired $\Lambda_m$ with $m>n$ and take $m\to\infty$. Both sides involve only fixed finite cylinder sums, proving the claimed Hamming inequality. [F1, F2, algebra]

1.5 We record the boundary bookkeeping for numerical duality. In a finite square with wired boundary, perimeter edges are quotient loops and are independent Bernoulli edges, so they can be omitted for interior cylinders. Collapse the perimeter to one vertex and keep the remaining edges, with the cyclic order inherited from the disk. Its faces are exactly the original unit-square cells; edges separating adjacent cells have the ordinary dual incidences. Thus its plane dual is the free rectangular grid on those cell centers. Applying [F5] to this quotient graph sends every retained primal edge to its complementary dual edge, with parameter $t^*$. These dual rectangles exhaust the translated dual square lattice; a fixed translate or one-cell outer-boundary shift is squeezed between the centered boxes with radii differing by a fixed constant. Finite boundary comparison and [F2] therefore give, for every dual cylinder $E$, $\pi^1_{t,q}(\text{dual-complement }E)=\pi^0_{t^*,q}(E)$. The dual graph includes no extra exterior vertex after this primal perimeter collapse; this is the free/wired interchange rather than a claim of torus self-duality. [F1, F2, F5, construct, algebra]

2.1 To turn this estimate into a bound for one specified rectangle, first take width $2u$, height $2bu$ with integer $b\geq1$, and torus side $L=16b^2u$. Let $B$ mean that some translate of a width-$u$, height-$L/2$ rectangle has a vertical crossing. It is translation invariant and has self-dual probability bounded below by [F3], since its fixed aspect is $8b^2$ and its height is strictly less than $L$. Every such narrow strip is contained horizontally in one of the width-$2u$ strips starting on the $u$-grid, and its height interval contains a full height-$2bu$ band starting on the $2bu$-grid. Its crossing therefore crosses one of $M=(L/u)(L/(2bu))$ fixed translates of the target rectangle. Wrapping translates are lifted to the plane for this containment. If their crossing events are $B_i$, positive association of their decreasing complements gives $(1-\phi_p(B_1))^M\leq\phi_p(\bigcap_iB_i^c)\leq\phi_p(B^c)$. Step 1.1 proves $\phi_p(B_1)\geq1-Cu^{-\eta/M}$. The number $M$ is independent of $u$. [F1, F3, F6, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 For a rectangle of width $w$ and height $h$ with $1\leq h/w\leq\beta$, take $u=\lfloor w/2\rfloor$ and a fixed integer $b$ depending only on $\beta$ with $2bu\geq h$. A crossing of the narrower, taller rectangle restricts to a crossing of the target. Rotating handles the other orientations. A fixed enlargement of $L/u$ in step 2.1 preserves the proof and accommodates any surrounding planar box of size comparable to $w$. Condition that torus law on all edges outside the box; its induced partition is bounded above by the wired partition. Hence the wired box gives the specified rectangle a crossing probability at least $1-Cw^{-\delta}$. The finitely many small widths are absorbed into $C$. [F1, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 Fix $\alpha>1$. For large $k$ put $a=r_k+2$, $b=r_{k+1}-2$, $R=r_{k+2}$. Use vertical crossings of $[a,b]\times[-b,b]$ and $[-b,-a]\times[-b,b]$, horizontal crossings of $[-b,b]\times[a,b]$ and $[-b,b]\times[-b,-a]$, and a horizontal crossing of $[-R,R]\times[-b,b]$. In each corner square the adjacent side crossings intersect by [F6]; their union contains a surrounding closed walk, from which erasing nonsurrounding loops gives a simple circuit. The last crossing intersects the two vertical sides and connects that circuit to the outer boundary. All widths are comparable to $\alpha^k$ and all aspects are fixed. Step 3.1 and a union bound give $\phi^1_{r_{k+2},p,q}(A_k)\geq1-d_k$ with $d_k=C e^{-\varepsilon k}$. Enlarge $K$ until $b>a$ and $d_k<1/2$ for $k\geq K$. [F6, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Suppose $A_{k+1},\ldots,A_n$ hold. Apply step 1.2 to the next annulus. The selected $\Gamma$ has an outgoing open connection to $\partial\Lambda_{r_{k+3}}$: an outgoing path from any surrounding circuit meets $\Gamma$. These outer events are measurable in its returned exterior data. For $A_{k+1}$ one may use $\Gamma$ itself, and any path excursion inside it can be replaced by an open circuit arc; circuits of $A_j$ for $j\geq k+2$ are outside it. On each output fiber, [F1] gives the interior FK law with all vertices of $\Gamma$ wired together by its actual open edges. Let $G_k(\Gamma)$ mean that a circuit of the inner annulus connects to $\Gamma$ inside its bounded domain. In wired $\Lambda_{r_{k+2}}$, $A_k$ implies $G_k(\Gamma)$ by separation, even when the fixed geometric $\Gamma$ is not open in that comparison law. Wired FK inside $\Gamma$ dominates the restriction of wired FK on the larger square. Step 4.1 therefore gives conditional probability at least $1-d_k$ for $G_k(\Gamma)$. Its connection then follows the already exposed outgoing path through $\Gamma$ to $\partial\Lambda_{r_{k+2}}$, giving $A_k$. Averaging the exterior fibers proves $P(A_k\mid A_{k+1},\ldots,A_n)\geq1-d_k$. No square boundary is asserted to be wired in the random configuration. [F1, F6, step 4.1, step 1.2, construct]

6.1 Start in wired $\Lambda_{r_{n+2}}$, where $A_n$ has probability at least $1-d_n$, and descend using step 5.1. This proves the finite product bound for $\bigcap_{k=N}^n A_k$, and hence for $\bigcap_{k=N}^m A_k$. For fixed $m$, take the deterministic outer-box limit along $n\to\infty$; finite additivity and $\prod_{k=N}^n(1-d_k)\geq1-\sum_{k=N}^n d_k$ prove the stated cylinder lower bound. No probability of an infinite intersection or measure extension is used. [F2, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 For $p>p_s$ choose $N\geq K$ with $\sum_{k\geq N}d_k\leq1/2$. Fix a deterministic nearest-neighbor tree containing all vertices of $\Lambda_{r_{N+1}}$; if it has $M_0$ edges, its all-open event $T$ has probability at least $\rho^{M_0}$ by successive edge conditioning. Finite FKG and step 6.1 give $\phi^1_{r_{n+2},p,q}(T\cap\bigcap_{k=N}^m A_k)\geq\rho^{M_0}/2$ for $n\geq m\geq N$. Consecutive circuits connect because an outgoing path meets the next surrounding circuit. For any prescribed $R$, take the least $m\geq N$ with $r_{m+2}>R$; this finite chain and the tree imply $D_R$. Taking only the outer-box limit gives $\pi^1_{p,q}(D_R)\geq\rho^{M_0}/2$ for every $R$, with the same constant. Step 1.3 proves $\Theta^1(p,q)>0$. [F1, F2, F6, step 6.1, step 1.3, construct]

7.2 Fix $s<p_s$ and choose one $t\in(s,p_s)$ such that $t^*\notin J_q$. The preimage of $J_q$ under the explicit dual bijection is countable. A point outside it can be specified without Countable Choice: enumerate that exceptional set, start with a rational closed interval inside $(s,p_s)$, and recursively take the first smaller rational closed interval in a fixed enumeration which avoids the next exceptional point and has diameter at most half the previous diameter. Its unique limit lies outside the exceptional set. Since $t^*>p_s$, step 6.1 at the dual parameter, for any chosen $\alpha>1$, supplies $N$ such that every finite intersection of dual annulus events with indices from $N$ onward has numerical wired weight at least $1/2$. By equality of the free/wired cylinder weights at $t^*$ and step 1.5, the same finite dual-circuit intersections have primal wired cylinder weight at least $1/2$ at $t$. [F2, step 6.1, step 1.5, construct]

8.1 Retain every other annulus, so its dual circuits have disjoint edge supports. Among the annuli strictly inside $\Lambda_{n-2}$ there are at least $(\log n)/(2\log\alpha)-O(N+1)$ retained circuits; the fixed dual-lattice translation changes only the cutoff. Every primal path realizing $D_n$ must cross each such circuit at a distinct closed primal edge. On the finite cylinder supporting these circuits and $H_n$, multiply this pointwise inequality by its nonnegative atom weights and sum. Step 7.2 gives $\mathbb E_{\pi^1_{t,q}}H_n\geq(\log n)/(8\log\alpha)$ for large $n$. Taking $\log\alpha=(t-s)/(4d+8)$ in step 1.4 gives $\pi^1_{s,q}(D_n)\leq n^{-(2d+4)}$ for sufficiently large $n$, proving the claimed bound after enlarging $C_d$. In particular these probabilities tend to zero, so step 1.3 yields $\Theta^1(s,q)=0$. All intersections and expectations used here are finite. [F6, step 1.3, step 1.4, step 7.2, algebra]

9.1 Every parameter strictly above $p_s$ belongs to the set defining the numerical threshold by step 7.1, and none strictly below belongs by step 8.1. Its infimum is therefore $p_s$. The proof never assigns a value at $p_s$ and never invokes an infinite-volume probability measure or Countable Choice. [step 7.1, step 8.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** The stated probability space and random families, with independence meaning factorization for every finite list of distinct sites.

[F1] Nonnegative integrals and their monotonicity are those of [[def-tdmath-measure-integral]].

[F2] Integrals commute with increasing nonnegative limits, so expectations of nonnegative countable sums are the sums of their expectations ([[thm-tdmath-monotone-convergence]]).



1.1 Every supremum defining $M_z$ is measurable because the roots are countable and each $S_y$ has countably many possible finite values. Translation of the common set law and [F2] give $\sum_yP(z\in S_y,|S_y|>u)=\mathbb E[|S_0|\mathbf1_{\{|S_0|>u\}}]$. This tail tends to zero: for example it is at most $u^{-1}\mathbb E|S_0|^2$. The union bound therefore shows $P(M_z>u)\to0$, hence $M_z<\infty$ almost surely. At least $S_z$ contains $z$, and every size is a positive integer, so a finite supremum is attained. Taking the countable union of the null exceptional events proves this simultaneously for all $z$. No independence of the $M_z$ is asserted. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 We first prove the assertion for the independent field $X$. Suppose sites are independently marked with probability $r$. If an animal of size at most $m$ contains $k$ distinct marked sites, a depth-first traversal of a spanning tree of that animal, rooted at $0$, visits them in some order using at most $2m$ steps. The successive displacement vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_k\in\mathbb Z^2$, starting at $0$, have total $\ell^1$ length at most $2m$. There are at most $2^{2k}\binom{2m+2k}{2k}\leq(Cm/k)^{2k}$ such ordered lists for $1\leq k\leq m$: choose signs of their two coordinates and distribute at most $2m$ units among $2k$ nonnegative coordinate magnitudes. Repeated sites and zero coordinates only cause overcounting. For a list of distinct visited sites, all its sites are marked with probability $r^k$. Thus $P(\text{some animal of size at most }m\text{ has }k\text{ marked sites})\leq(C' r m^2/k^2)^k$. This counts marked-site lists rather than all animals and is uniform over all their shapes. [given, construct, algebra]

2.1 Put $m=2^l$, $r_j=P(X_0\geq2^j)$ and fix $\epsilon=1/4$. Choose a deterministic $a$ such that $C'/a^2\leq e^{-2}$, and a fixed $B\geq2$. For $0\leq j\leq\lfloor\epsilon\log_2m\rfloor$ set $k_j=\lceil\max\{am\sqrt{r_j},B\log m\}\rceil$. If $k_j>m$ the corresponding forbidden event is empty; otherwise step 1.2 bounds its probability by $e^{-2k_j}\leq m^{-2B}$. The union over these $O(\log m)$ values of $j$ is summable along dyadic $m$. For a moment order $Q>2/\epsilon$, the elementary inequality $P(X_0>v)\leq v^{-Q}\mathbb E X_0^Q$ and the fact that every size-at-most-$m$ animal lies in $\Lambda_m=[-m,m]^2\cap\mathbb Z^2$ give $P(\max_{\Lambda_m}X_y>m^\epsilon)\leq(2m+1)^2\mathbb E X_0^Q m^{-\epsilon Q}$, also summable in $l$. [F1, step 1.2, choose, algebra]

3.1 If events $E_l$ have summable probabilities, then $P(\bigcup_{l\geq L}E_l)\leq\sum_{l\geq L}P(E_l)\to0$; countable additivity implies that only finitely many $E_l$ occur almost surely. Apply this elementary argument to the failures in step 2.1. Almost surely, for every sufficiently large dyadic $m$, all weights in $\Lambda_m$ are at most $m^\epsilon$, and every size-at-most-$m$ animal has fewer than $k_j$ sites with $X_y\geq2^j$ at each relevant level. The pointwise layer bound $X_y\leq1+\sum_{j\geq0}2^{j+1}\mathbf1_{\{X_y\geq2^j\}}$ then gives, for every animal with $m/2<|\Gamma|\leq m$, $|\Gamma|^{-1}\sum_{y\in\Gamma}X_y\leq1+4a\sum_{j\geq0}2^j\sqrt{r_j}+O(m^{\epsilon-1}\log m)$. Levels above $\epsilon\log_2m$ contribute zero; the error comes from the additive $B\log m+1$ in $k_j$. The constants are deterministic. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 A fixed moment order $Q>2$ gives $\sqrt{r_j}\leq(\mathbb E X_0^Q)^{1/2}2^{-Qj/2}$, so the series in step 3.1 converges. Its value is deterministic, and the error tends to zero. Choose $K$ larger than $2+4a\sum_{j\geq0}2^j\sqrt{r_j}$. Every sufficiently large animal belongs to one of the dyadic size ranges in step 3.1. Thus almost surely its average $X$-weight is at most this same $K$, proving the general independent-field assertion. [F1, step 3.1, choose, algebra]

5.1 Apply step 4.1 to $X_y=|S_y|^2$, which is an independent identically distributed field with all moments. Work on the probability-one event where its large-animal bound holds and all $M_z$ are finite. Let $\Gamma$ be any sufficiently large animal, $m=|\Gamma|$, $A=\sum_{z\in\Gamma}M_z$, and $t=A/(2m)>0$. For each of the finitely many $z\in\Gamma$ with $M_z>t$, choose a root $y(z)$ attaining its maximum; to avoid even a selection convention take the first such root in a fixed enumeration of $\mathbb Z^2$. Let $Y$ be the distinct chosen roots, $s_y=|S_y|$, $U=\sum_{y\in Y}s_y^2$, and $V=\sum_{y\in Y}s_y$. Low-weight sites contribute at most $A/2$, and at most $s_y$ sites can be assigned to a given $S_y$. Hence $U\geq A/2=mt$. Since $s_y>t$ for chosen roots, $V\leq U/t$. [step 1.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 The set $\Delta=\Gamma\cup\bigcup_{y\in Y}S_y$ is a finite connected animal containing every root in $Y$, because every chosen set meets $\Gamma$ and is connected. Its size is at least $m$ and at most $m+V$. Therefore the same large-animal bound gives $U\leq\sum_{y\in\Delta}|S_y|^2\leq K|\Delta|\leq K(m+U/t)$. If $t>2K$, this would imply $U<2Km$ while step 5.1 gives $U\geq mt>2Km$, a contradiction. Thus $t\leq2K$ and $A\leq4Km$. Taking the deterministic constant $K_0=4K$ proves the envelope assertion uniformly over every sufficiently large animal. Only the given probability laws and countable additivity were used, without constructing any new infinite family. [step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Countable Choice, real $q\geq1$, a sub-self-dual parameter, and the actual free/wired Borel laws extending their finite-cylinder limits.

[A1] Countable Choice is the axiom in [[def-countable-choice]]. It is spent in the indicated measure-extension and countable-kernel steps, without invoking arbitrary-index choice or dependent choice.

[F1] The actual free/wired probability laws exist under [A1] and have the numerical cylinder weights supplied by [[lem-csm-frontier-fk-free-wired-limits]] and [[lem-csm-frontier-fk-cylinder-pressure-comparison]]; cylinder-limit states are defined in [[def-csm-frontier-fk-infinite-volume-states]].

[F2] Finite FK has spatial Markov, association, common-uniform heat-bath monotone couplings, and parameter/boundary comparison ([[lem-csm-frontier-fk-fkg-spatial-markov]]).

[F3] For every sub-self-dual $s$ and $d>0$, the numerical one-arm bound is $\pi^1_{s,q}(D_n)\leq C_d n^{-(2d+4)}$ for large $n$; for $p<s$, $\pi^1_{p,q}(D_n)\leq\exp\{-4(s-p)\mathbb E_{\pi^1_{s,q}}H_n\}$, where $H_n$ is finite Hamming distance to $D_n$ ([[lem-csm-frontier-fk-wired-annuli-and-numerical-threshold]]). Its proof supplies all annulus ratios and intermediate nonexceptional dual parameters, without a critical-state assumption.

[F4] Given independent shifted finite connected sets with all size moments on a probability space, their envelope has a deterministic uniform large-animal average bound ([[lem-csm-frontier-fk-independent-cluster-animal-envelope]]).

[F5] Under [A1], consistent finite-alphabet probabilities on a countable coordinate set extend uniquely to a probability law, and such laws have cylinder-convergent subsequences ([[lem-csm-lattice-product-and-measure-compactness]]).

[F6] Nonnegative monotone convergence and Fatou's inequality hold on the actual measure spaces ([[thm-tdmath-monotone-convergence]], [[lem-tdmath-fatou]]).



1.1 Fix any $s<p_s:=\sqrt q/(1+\sqrt q)$ and let $R_x=\sup\{\lVert z-x\rVert_\infty:z\in C_x\}$, allowing infinity initially. The event $R_x\geq n$ is the translate of $D_n$: a path reaching that distance has an initial segment inside the centered box to its boundary. Its probability under the wired law is its numerical cylinder weight by [F1]. Thus [F3], with arbitrarily large $d$, gives polynomial tails of arbitrarily high order for $R_x$. Since $|C_x|\leq(2R_x+1)^2$, nonnegative monotone convergence applied to successive integer layers proves $\mathbb E_s^1|C_x|^d<\infty$ for every $d>0$; explicitly the layer bound for $R_x^{2d}$ is a constant times $\sum_{n\geq1}n^{2d-1}P(R_x\geq n)$, which converges after choosing [F3] with that $d$. Every $C_x$ is finite almost surely, simultaneously at all countably many vertices. Translation invariance follows from the numerical cylinder identities in [F1] and uniqueness in [F5]. [F1, F3, F5, F6, algebra]

2.1 We establish a conditional cluster comparison before constructing a new law. Enumerate the vertices deterministically. Suppose a finite number of complete finite clusters have been discovered, with union $E$. Revealing their vertex sets says that each discovered set is connected by its internal open edges and every edge from it to its complement is closed. These are finite-edge events. In each finite FK box, after all edges between $E$ and its complement are fixed closed, the component factors and edge weights internal to $E$ factor from the remaining weights; summing over allowed internal configurations preserves that factorization. Hence the law outside $E$ depends on the discovered sets only through the closed boundary edges. Passing fixed finite-cylinder conditional probabilities to the wired limit proves the same identity there. A positive-probability history has a positive denominator because its defining finite edge event does; null histories may be assigned arbitrary normalized kernels and are never reached. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

3.1 If the next vertex $y$ is outside $E$, its conditional cluster law is dominated, by inclusion of vertex sets, by the unconditional wired cluster law of $y$. Indeed in a finite box compare the original wired law with the same law constrained to close every edge from $E$ to its complement. The common-uniform heat-bath update in [F2] preserves order; fixed-closed coordinates stay below the upper chain, and all other conditional edge probabilities remain ordered. Taking stationary limits gives an ordered finite-box coupling. Apply [F5] to the pair of binary edge fields along growing boxes and take a joint cylinder limit. Its upper marginal is the wired law; its lower marginal outside $E$ is the conditional law in step 2.1, since conditioning a fixed positive-probability cylinder commutes with these limits. The order event is a countable intersection of coordinatewise closed conditions and holds in the limit. Project to the two clusters of $y$. Both are finite almost surely, by the upper marginal and step 1.1. This proves existence of an ordered coupling on pairs of finite connected vertex sets for each possible positive-probability history. [A1, F2, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 The possible finite histories, finite connected lattice sets, and pairs of such sets have explicit countable encodings by integer vertex lists. Apply [A1] to the fixed countable family of nonempty sets of coupling kernels from step 3.1, choosing one kernel for every history in advance. At a stage whose vertex $y$ is already discovered, its actual-cluster output is its earlier cluster and the second output is a fresh independent set with the unconditional cluster law of $y$. At an undiscovered $y$, use its selected ordered kernel: its first marginal is the conditional cluster law from step 2.1 and its second marginal is again that fixed unconditional law. Each kernel is a probability on a countable set of pairs of finite sets. The product of the successive kernels defines normalized consistent finite-prefix atomic probabilities; summing the last kernel's mass one verifies consistency. A kernel's second marginal is fixed for every history, including the earlier second outputs, so these second outputs have product marginals for every finite list of stages. Countable Choice here selects kernels for a countable set fixed in advance, rather than successive unspecified choices from a relation. [A1, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 Here is an explicit extension of the process, to avoid assuming a countable-alphabet extension theorem. Enumerate each stage's possible output pairs by integers $j\geq0$, and encode $j$ by a bit row consisting of $j$ ones, a zero, and then zeros. For every finite set of coordinates in the countable array of bits, sum the appropriate finite-prefix atomic probabilities from step 4.1. All sums are nonnegative countable sums over explicitly enumerated finite tuples of integers. Summing the last kernel verifies consistency of the binary finite-dimensional laws. Identify the bit array with the countable coordinates in [F5] and extend under [A1]. For a given row the weight of its first $K$ bits being all ones is the atomic tail $P(j\geq K)$, tending to zero, so the all-ones row has probability zero by countable additivity. Each finite pattern having a one after its first zero also has prescribed probability zero. A countable union shows that almost surely every row is a valid integer code. Decode on this measurable full-probability set, assigning a fixed default on its null complement. The resulting process has exactly the specified finite-prefix laws. This constructs the required law without an additional invocation of a process-extension or independent-uniform theorem. [A1, F5, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

6.1 Write $S_y$ for the second output at the stage of $y$, and $\widehat C_z$ for the actual cluster assigned by the first outputs. Step 4.1 shows that the $S_y-y$ are independent and identically distributed as the translated wired cluster; their sizes have all moments by step 1.1. The first outputs have precisely the original wired cluster-exploration laws by induction on every finite prefix. The complete cluster at each fixed $z$ is assigned by the stage reaching $z$, so all finite lists of complete cluster sets have the actual wired joint law. Equality of the whole countably indexed cluster-set law follows as well: unary encode these finite-set labels; its binary cylinder values determine its law uniquely by [F5]. Whenever a new cluster is discovered at $y$, it is a subset of $S_y$ by the ordered kernel. Every $z$ in that cluster therefore satisfies $|\widehat C_z|\leq M_z:=\sup\{|S_y|:z\in S_y\}$. The enumeration eventually assigns every vertex. This coupled object is a cluster partition, not an edge configuration reconstructed from clusters. [F5, step 1.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct, algebra]

7.1 Apply [F4] to the given independent family $S_y$ on the constructed probability space. There is a deterministic finite $K_0$ such that almost surely all sufficiently large animals $\Gamma$ satisfy $\sum_{z\in\Gamma}|\widehat C_z|\leq\sum_{z\in\Gamma}M_z\leq K_0|\Gamma|$. This countably measurable property of the cluster partition transfers to the actual wired law by step 6.1. An animal is a finite connected vertex set containing $0$, so this applies simultaneously to every sufficiently long self-avoiding path starting at $0$. No claim that the dependent envelope variables are independent is made. [F4, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 In any edge configuration with such a cluster partition, let $\gamma$ be a self-avoiding path from $0$ to $\partial\Lambda_n$, with $m$ vertices. It has $m\geq n+1$. If it visits $J$ distinct open clusters, its number $T(\gamma)$ of closed edges is at least $J-1$. Each visited cluster $C$ contributes at most one to $\sum_{z\in\gamma}|C_z|^{-1}$, because the path visits distinct vertices. Cauchy–Schwarz therefore gives $T(\gamma)+1\geq\sum_{z\in\gamma}|C_z|^{-1}\geq m^2/(\sum_{z\in\gamma}|C_z|)\geq m/K_0$ for all sufficiently long paths, by step 7.1. The subtraction of one is necessary even for a path contained in a single cluster. Since this inequality holds for every edge configuration with that partition, transferring the partition law was sufficient; no internal open edges had to be selected in the coupling. [step 7.1, algebra]

9.1 A path minimizing the number of closed edges in the finite box may be taken self-avoiding by erasing loops without increasing that number. The uniform large-animal cutoff in step 7.1 and step 8.1 give $H_n\geq(n+1)/K_0-1$ for all sufficiently large $n$, almost surely in the actual wired law at $s$. Fatou's inequality from [F6], applied to the nonnegative measurable variables $H_n/n$, gives $\liminf_n\mathbb E_s^1H_n/n\geq1/K_0$. Thus for all sufficiently large deterministic $n$, $\mathbb E_s^1H_n\geq n/(2K_0)$. This expectation conclusion does not assume a deterministic bound on the random almost-sure cutoff. [F6, step 7.1, step 8.1, algebra]

10.1 Now fix the parameter $p$ in the statement and choose $s\in(p,p_s)$. Steps 1.1–3.3 apply at this $s$. Since $H_n$ is a finite-coordinate function, its expectation under the wired Borel law is exactly the finite sum of its numerical cylinder atom weights in [F3]. That supplier's Hamming inequality therefore gives $\phi^1_{p,q}(D_n)\leq\exp\{-2(s-p)n/K_0\}$ for sufficiently large $n$. Increasing a prefactor covers all $n\geq1$. In particular the probability of an infinite cluster at $0$ is zero: that event is contained in every $D_n$, whose probabilities tend to zero. [F1, F3, step 9.1, choose, algebra]

11.1 By translation invariance, the same one-arm bound holds at every center. If $x\ne y$ and $r=\lVert x-y\rVert_\infty$, any finite open path from $x$ to $y$ has an initial segment from $x$ to the vertex boundary of $x+\Lambda_r$ inside that box. Thus its wired connection probability is at most the translated one-arm bound at radius $r$. Since $r\geq\lVert x-y\rVert_2/\sqrt2$, changing constants proves $\phi^1_{p,q}(x\leftrightarrow y)\leq C(p,q)e^{-c(p,q)\lVert x-y\rVert_2}$, also for $x=y$ after enlarging $C$. [F1, step 10.1, algebra]

12.1 Let $\phi$ be any cylinder limit in the statement. An increasing event supported on a fixed inner box has finite-volume conditional laws with boundary partitions at most wired; passing its cylinder probabilities to the limit bounds them above by the wired inner-box law. Then increase that inner box to infinity, using the wired cylinder limit in [F1], to obtain domination by the wired state on increasing cylinder events. The event that $x$ connects $y$ by a path in a fixed box is such an event. These events increase to $\{x\leftrightarrow y\}$ as boxes grow; countable additivity, or [F6] applied to their indicators, therefore gives the identical upper bound in step 11.1 for $\phi$. Similarly the translated $D_n$ events dominate any infinite cluster at their center, giving probability zero. Constants depend only on $p,q$, not on the cylinder-limit state. The proof has made no assertion at $p_s$ and has used Countable Choice exactly in the stated extensions and kernel selection. [A1, F1, F2, F6, step 10.1, step 11.1, algebra] ∎
